messages.subject: Re: mixedmirt (random intercept)
messages.body_plain:
> Or alternatively can mirt() allows for covariates (latent regression)?

Also yes, but does not support random effects (and probably never will). fscores() will also account for the latent structures in mirt(), allowing for plausible values and other related methods. Cheers.

Assume my model is a three-dimensional model (one item measures only one dimension; between-item design) and I want to include covariates. Could I assign different covariates to the three dimensions respectively? For example, gender to dimension1, age to dimension 2, education to dimension 3. Thanks. Here I mean using mirt().

messages.subject: Re: mixedmirt (random intercept)
messages.body_plain:
For the mirt() function, in theory yes, though I haven't implemented support for such an approach yet. Currently all regression coefficients are modelled for each trait at once. This probably meets your goal for now, at the cost of a slight decrease in power for including needless fixed effects.

In mixedmirt(), the latest dev version can support this through the lr.fixed input, though it may be buggy as it is not well tested yet. And alternatively, if the model is Rasch then creating a suitable itemdesign effect for each factor and interacting it with the between-group effects would generate a suitable fixed/random coefficient to do the job.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: mixedmirt (random intercept)
messages.body_plain:
You need a fixed = ~ group + X, or whatever R formula added to that. Also, in mirt() the latent regression is only available for the EM algorithm (that's why the mirt and mixedmirt functions currently differ; the estimators deal with the problem rather differently). If you are running a later dev, there should be an example at the bottom of the ?mirt help file. Cheers.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: sample and test items ratio
messages.body_plain:
Hi Somayeh,

On Sun, Nov 30, 2014 at 8:54 AM, somayeh shahba <so.s...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Philip,
>
> I have question regarding sample and test items.As you know when we want to use some classical software for analyzing our data we need 10-15 times sample more than our items.for example 100 items need 1000 to 1500 sample to answer. dose this ratio exist in IRT when we identify item repose theory non sensitive to sample or sample dependency?

I'm not sure where those ratios came from, but I doubt even they should be trusted. Rules of thumb are great for determining simple a priori power, but the best way to determine the required power is to run some simulation results, which given the speed of modern computers really isn't much of an issue anymore. This especially so in IRT where item-level models can differ (i.e., the Rasch model likely requires substantially smaller sample sizes than the 2PL, and the 3- and 4PL models require samples well into the thousands for decent parameters estimates....polytomous items a similar story, where even the number of categories is a factor).

So I would generally avoid trying to find a rule of thumb in IRT, or any statistical model for that matter, and simply determine the power ranges yourself. Cheers.

Phil

>
> Regards,
>
> Somayeh

messages.subject: Re: a-parameter in bifactor model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Yutaro,

Yes, slope parameters can be negative, and in bifactor models this often happens in the specific factors. It's nothing to worry about since slopes are 'partial regression coefficients', so the results are in no way paradoxical. Cheers.

Phil

Phil

My question is: can I set 'mirt' package to NMAR or MAR to estimate the items parameters? My data is dichotomous, N > 1,000.

I think that because time was very short to do all 110 items, NMAR can be observed.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Danilo,

On Thu, Dec 4, 2014 at 4:10 PM, Danilo Assis Pereira <dani...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi, Dr. Phil,
>
>
> I have two different missing values patterns in my data (two different educational tests). The first one is NMAR (not missing-at-random), and the second one is MAR (missing-at-random), as can be seen in the pictures. My question is: can I set 'mirt' package to NMAR or MAR to estimate the items parameters? My data is dichotomous, N > 1,000.
>
> I think that because time was very short to do all 110 items, NMAR can be observed.

You're right there is definitely a time effect going on here, where after about the 60th item missingness seems to consistently increase. However, this in and of itself may not be an issue depending on the missingness mechanism, and MAR could very well be a reasonable assumption (which is mirt's default). Let me explain.

If the only reason individuals have difficulty answering those last items is because of individual differences in the time it takes to answer items, then MAR is a reasonable assumption and the estimation would simply take into account that there are less observations for those items, and in turn their parameter sampling variability will be much higher (i.e., have higher standard errors). However, if there is a reason other than time that is responsible for these missing data patterns, then MNAR is an issue. More specifically, for example: are the students with higher abilities more likely to answer those last few questions compared to the rest of the students? Lower ability students more likely? Is there any visual relationship between the score estimates and missing data pattern? Etc. The point is that time by itself really is not an issue in MAR here, it's whether some individuals are more likely to response based on their innate ability. And if there are observable biases based on the latent trait scores, then MAR is being violated and there's little you can do about it without making some rather dogmatic assumptions. If MAR is violated, you may have to count your losses and discard the last half of the test.

My suggestion would be to continue to look into the problem using regression-based methods. Perhaps using the first 60 items only, compute latent trait estimates for individuals and try and discern whether there is a relationship to the probability of attempting the items in the last half of the test. If the relationships end up being small or insignificant, then MNAR may not be an issue and the MAR assumption is still fairly reasonable.

Note that for policy reasons, you probably should also look at other demographic variables as well to see if they predict the missingness (i.e., were males more likely to answer more questions than females, primary speaking language more likely to answer more, etc). Though these really don't effect the parameter estimation, directly in order to justify keeping them for the future you would want those to be non-significant as well (otherwise you'd bias the number of items administered for one sub-population over another...which is difficult to justify). Good luck.

Phil

>
> Thanks a lot,
>
>
>  <https://lh4.googleusercontent.com/-WZ8yI81iwEY/VIDMX2scAPI/AAAAAAAABiY/UhSpqD-wFxs/s1600/not_missing_at_random.png>
>
>
>  <https://lh6.googleusercontent.com/-7xk2iUPcTOg/VIDMShSTBDI/AAAAAAAABiQ/nxAvYmyMbkM/s1600/missin_at_random.png>
>

messages.subject: Re: a-parameter in bifactor model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,Phil

I'm continue to do bifactor model analysis in mirt.
(I want to check dimensionality using bifactor model and MIRT.)

I analyzed some data(all items=25,N=9000) and coef() is;

$X02item23
    a1 a2    a3    a4     d g u
par  0  0 0.206 1.602 0.346 0 1

$X02item24
    a1 a2     a3     a4     d g u
par  0  0 13.278 10.688 7.129 0 1

$X02item25
    a1 a2    a3    a4     d g u
par  0  0 0.933 1.594 0.321 0 1

In item24, a-para is very large...but I calculate factor loading;
                  F1    F2    F3    h2
X02item23 0.000 0.000 0.700 0.491
X02item24 0.000 0.000 0.676 0.457
X02item25 0.000 0.000 0.689 0.475

Could that happen?

I'm worrying about that.

thank you.

2014年12月3日水曜日 15時46分28秒 UTC+9 Phil Chalmers:

> Hi Yutaro,

>
> Yes, slope parameters can be negative, and in bifactor models this often happens in the specific factors. It's nothing to worry about since slopes are 'partial regression coefficients', so the results are in no way paradoxical. Cheers.
>
> Phil

>
> On Wed, Dec 3, 2014 at 1:33 AM, Yutaro Sakamoto <s.ich...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > I'm trying to do bifactor model and estimate a-parameter in G ,F1, F2, F3 factor in mirt.
> >
> > Today I estimated that ,but a-parameter got minus.
> >
> > In bifactor model, could a-parameter get minus?
> >
> > Thanks.

messages.subject: Re: mixedmirt (random intercept)
messages.body_plain:
I don't think it's possible. Missing values in the independent variables are pretty hard to deal with (same issue occurs in standard regression analyses). Probably the best approach would be to impute them using multiple imputation methods and average over multiple sets. Sorry.

Phil

On Fri, Dec 5, 2014 at 1:06 AM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thank you, Phil. It seems mixedmirt does not allow missing values in continuous or categorical covariates. Will it support in the future? Say, missing at random?
>
> Phil Chalmers於 2014年12月4日星期四UTC+8下午12時10分19秒寫道：
> > Yes, the syntax looks good, and mixedmirt()'s lr.fixed input can tell how to use the variables (the standard R formula input deals with that using the usual R matrix.model() functions and such).
> >
> > Phil
> >
> > On Wed, Dec 3, 2014 at 11:01 PM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Thank you, Phil. Let say if adding covariate like gender (male and female) to second factor, I am not sure if mixedmirt(resp, covdata, cmodel, lr.fixed = list(F2=~ gender) ) is fine? Can lr.fixed tell the covariate is continuous or categorical?
> > >
> > >
> > > Phil Chalmers於 2014年12月3日星期三UTC+8下午12時46分55秒寫道：
> > > >
> > > > On Tue, Dec 2, 2014 at 1:44 AM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > I have five-dimensional data, every 14 items measure one dimension. First, I tried estimate the last two dimension with one covariate regressed on last dimension, pseudoIQ. Syntax is as follows:
> > > > >
> > > > > dim0 = 2
> > > > > itemnum = 14
> > > > >
> > > > > Q <- array( 0 , dim = c( dim0*itemnum , dim0 ))
> > > > > ind = numeric()
> > > > > for (c in 1:dim0){
> > > > >     ind = c( ind, rep(c,itemnum) )
> > > > > }
> > > > > Q[cbind(1:(dim0*itemnum), ind)] <- 1
> > > > >
> > > > > COV = matrix(TRUE, dim0, dim0)
> > > > > cmodel <- mirt.model(Q, COV=COV)
> > > > > pseudoIQ <- read.table("pseudoIQ.txt", col.names="pseudoIQ")
> > > > > covdata <- data.frame(pseudoIQ)
> > > > >
> > > > > resp <- read.table("resp.txt")
> > > > > cmod <- mirt(resp[,43:70], cmodel, covdata=covdata, formula = list(F2=~ pseudoIQ) , itemtype='Rasch', SE=TRUE, method = "EM", SE.type="crossprod")
> > > > > est = coef(cmod, printSE = TRUE, as.data.frame = TRUE)
> > > > >
> > > > > But it estimated for F1 and F2:
> > > > > $lr.betas
> > > > >                F1    F2
> > > > > (Intercept) 0.000 0.000
> > > > > pseudoIQ    0.041 0.516
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Patched now. Thanks.
> > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Second, I tried to estimate all five-dimensional data with one covariate regressed on last dimension, pseudoIQ.
> > > > >
> > > > > dim0 = 5
> > > > > itemnum = 14
> > > > >
> > > > > Q <- array( 0 , dim = c( dim0*itemnum , dim0 ))
> > > > > ind = numeric()
> > > > > for (c in 1:dim0){
> > > > >     ind = c( ind, rep(c,itemnum) )
> > > > > }
> > > > > Q[cbind(1:(dim0*itemnum), ind)] <- 1
> > > > >
> > > > > COV = matrix(TRUE, dim0, dim0)
> > > > > cmodel <- mirt.model(Q, COV=COV)
> > > > > pseudoIQ <- read.table("pseudoIQ.txt", col.names="pseudoIQ")
> > > > > covdata <- data.frame(pseudoIQ)
> > > > >
> > > > > resp <- read.table("resp.txt")
> > > > > cmod <- mirt(resp, cmodel, covdata=covdata, formula = list(F5=~ pseudoIQ) , itemtype='Rasch', SE=TRUE, method = "EM", SE.type="crossprod")
> > > > > est = coef(cmod, printSE = TRUE, as.data.frame = TRUE)
> > > > >
> > > > > But there was a error:
> > > > > Iteration: 22, Log-Lik: -48215.200, Max-Change: 0.04489Error in solve.default(sigma) :
> > > > >   system is computationally singular: reciprocal condition number = 5.21813e-18
> > > >
> > > > The latent variables in this model are quite highly correlated, and using EM estimation the quadrature become too problematic to deal with (the number of points is reduce to only 3 per dimension....so quite inaccurate). mixedmirt() seems to estimate this fine though, since the MHRM is generally better at dealing with high dimensional and multicollinear models. Cheers.
> > > >
> > > > Phil
> > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Phil Chalmers於 2014年12月2日星期二UTC+8上午12時18分17秒寫道：
> > > > > > Okay, this has been added. Simply pass a named list of formula to mirt(..., formula = list(...)) or mixedmirt(..., lr.fixed=list(...)), where the names correspond to the factor names defined in 'model'. Cheers.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Phil
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Mon, Dec 1, 2014 at 1:26 AM, Phil Chalmers <rphilip....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > You need a fixed = ~ group + X, or whatever R formula added to that. Also, in mirt() the latent regression is only available for the EM algorithm (that's why the mirt and mixedmirt functions currently differ; the estimators deal with the problem rather differently). If you are running a later dev, there should be an example at the bottom of the ?mirt help file. Cheers.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Mon, Dec 1, 2014 at 1:22 AM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > Thanks, Phil. I have tried mirt() by including covariates:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > covdata <- data.frame(pseudoIQ)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > cmod <- mirt(resp, cmodel, covdata=covdata, itemtype='Rasch', SE=TRUE, method = "MHRM", technical=list(BURNIN=1000,SEMCYCLES=100,NCYCLES=10000), SE.type="")
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > coef(cmod)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > But, I didn't see the estimate of coefficient.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Phil Chalmers於 2014年12月1日星期一UTC+8下午1時33分40秒寫道：
> > > > > > > > > For the mirt() function, in theory yes, though I haven't implemented support for such an approach yet. Currently all regression coefficients are modelled for each trait at once. This probably meets your goal for now, at the cost of a slight decrease in power for including needless fixed effects.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > In mixedmirt(), the latest dev version can support this through the lr.fixed input, though it may be buggy as it is not well tested yet. And alternatively, if the model is Rasch then creating a suitable itemdesign effect for each factor and interacting it with the between-group effects would generate a suitable fixed/random coefficient to do the job.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > On Mon, Dec 1, 2014 at 12:17 AM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > Or alternatively can mirt() allows for covariates (latent regression)?
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Also yes, but does not support random effects (and probably never will). fscores() will also account for the latent structures in mirt(), allowing for plausible values and other related methods. Cheers.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Assume my model is a three-dimensional model (one item measures only one dimension; between-item design) and I want to include covariates. Could I assign different covariates to the three dimensions respectively? For example, gender to dimension1, age to dimension 2, education to dimension 3. Thanks.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Phil Chalmers於 2014年11月27日星期四UTC+8下午10時35分24秒寫道：
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > On Thu, Nov 27, 2014 at 3:08 AM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > > Thank you, Phil. Now it works well. By the way, can mixedmirt() handle multidimensional IRT? Say, only one major trait is treated in multilevel structure and others are ignored.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Yes, but specific decomposition of the traits is not yet supported. One can get around this by including general intercept differences, but these will largely be agnostic to the multidimensional traits used (which has pros and cons). Ability decomposition support will be coming at a later time.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Or alternatively can mirt() allows for covariates (latent regression)?
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Also yes, but does not support random effects (and probably never will). fscores() will also account for the latent structures in mirt(), allowing for plausible values and other related methods. Cheers.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Phil Chalmers於 2014年11月27日星期四UTC+8上午12時52分26秒寫道：
> > > > > > > > > > > > > Indeed, there was an inadvertent line of code causing issues in the draw variability (causing severe shrinkage towards the mean). This is now patched, and the simulation returns the following results now.
> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > summary(mod1)
> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > Call:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > mixedmirt(data = data, covdata = covdata, model = 1, fixed = ~0 +
> > > > > > > > > > > > >     items, random = ~1 | group)
> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > --------------
> > > > > > > > > > > > > RANDOM EFFECT COVARIANCE(S):
> > > > > > > > > > > > > Correlations on upper diagonal
> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > $Theta
> > > > > > > > > > > > >     F1
> > > > > > > > > > > > > F1 1.1
> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > $group
> > > > > > > > > > > > >           COV_group
> > > > > > > > > > > > > COV_group     0.878
> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > So the SD estimates are now sqrt(1.1) = 1.048, and sqrt(.878) = 0.937, which are much more reasonable. Thanks for the report!
> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Hi Phil,
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > I experienced a hard time understanding what is working on behind mixedmirt. For simplicity, I simulated a random intercept data, where sample size 3000, group=200, using Rasch model, and the syntax is as follows:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > ~~~~~~
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > rm(list=ls())
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > set.seed(1234)
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > N <- 3000
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > a <- matrix(rep(1,10),10,1) # all ones
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > d <- matrix(seq(-2,2,length.out=10),10,1); d[1] = 0
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > cluster = 200
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > random_intercept = rnorm(cluster,0,1)
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Theta = numeric()
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > for (i in 1:cluster){
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > >     Theta <- c(Theta, rnorm(N/cluster,0,1) + random_intercept[i])
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > >     }
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > group = factor(rep(paste0('G',1:cluster), each = N/cluster))
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > covdata <- data.frame(group)
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > data <- simdata(a,d,N, itemtype = rep('dich',10), Theta=matrix(Theta))
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > mod1 <- mixedmirt(data, covdata, 1, fixed = ~ 0 + items, random = ~ 1|group)
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > coef(mod1, printSE = TRUE)
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > ~~~~~~
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > The item estimates were fine, but the variance of theta and variance of random intercept were not 1 and 1:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > $GroupPars
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > >     MEAN_1 COV_11

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > SE      NA    NaN
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > $group
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > >     COV_group_group

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > SE              NaN
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Not sure if I simulated incorrectly?
> > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > This looks like it should work, so I'm not sure why it isn't coming up with the correct estimates. I'll look into it and let you know what I find.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > How to estimate the mean of random intercept? (and put constrain on item estimate, overall mean is zero)
> > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > You can't, mainly because by convention random effects are generally thought to be centered at 0, and therefore I don't allow for them to be estimated. Cheers.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Thank you~

On Fri, Dec 5, 2014 at 1:31 AM, Yutaro Sakamoto <s.ich...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi,Phil
>

> Now I updated mirt package but the same thing happened...

> X02item23

> and summary();

> X02item23  0.0000 0.0000  0.08766 0.683 0.474
> X02item24  0.0000 0.0000  0.77457 0.625 0.991
> X02item25  0.0000 0.0000  0.37116 0.635 0.541

This looks better now (h2, the commonality, is closer to what it should be). This looks to be a type of Heywood case with in IRT flavour, where the slopes are tending to infinity and hence the commonality is very close to 1. It's hard to know what a reasonable solution to this problem is (priors can help keep them down at the cost of bias, or dropping the specific factor loading can help....but may decrease model fit in an unacceptable way). Dealing with an item like that will require some judgment outside of what I can offer statistically. Sorry.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: MAR and NMAR missing
messages.body_plain:
Thank you very much, Dr. Phil! You helped me to understand better the problem, and I will try to find out if there is bias in the last half of the test.

Bests,

Danilo

2014-12-04 21:54 GMT-02:00 Phil Chalmers <rphilip....@gmail.com>:
> Hi Danilo,
>
> On Thu, Dec 4, 2014 at 4:10 PM, Danilo Assis Pereira <dani...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi, Dr. Phil,
> >
> >
> > I have two different missing values patterns in my data (two different educational tests). The first one is NMAR (not missing-at-random), and the second one is MAR (missing-at-random), as can be seen in the pictures. My question is: can I set 'mirt' package to NMAR or MAR to estimate the items parameters? My data is dichotomous, N > 1,000.
> >
> > I think that because time was very short to do all 110 items, NMAR can be observed.
>
> You're right there is definitely a time effect going on here, where after about the 60th item missingness seems to consistently increase. However, this in and of itself may not be an issue depending on the missingness mechanism, and MAR could very well be a reasonable assumption (which is mirt's default). Let me explain.
>
> If the only reason individuals have difficulty answering those last items is because of individual differences in the time it takes to answer items, then MAR is a reasonable assumption and the estimation would simply take into account that there are less observations for those items, and in turn their parameter sampling variability will be much higher (i.e., have higher standard errors). However, if there is a reason other than time that is responsible for these missing data patterns, then MNAR is an issue. More specifically, for example: are the students with higher abilities more likely to answer those last few questions compared to the rest of the students? Lower ability students more likely? Is there any visual relationship between the score estimates and missing data pattern? Etc. The point is that time by itself really is not an issue in MAR here, it's whether some individuals are more likely to response based on their innate ability. And if there are observable biases based on the latent trait scores, then MAR is being violated and there's little you can do about it without making some rather dogmatic assumptions. If MAR is violated, you may have to count your losses and discard the last half of the test.
>
> My suggestion would be to continue to look into the problem using regression-based methods. Perhaps using the first 60 items only, compute latent trait estimates for individuals and try and discern whether there is a relationship to the probability of attempting the items in the last half of the test. If the relationships end up being small or insignificant, then MNAR may not be an issue and the MAR assumption is still fairly reasonable.
>
> Note that for policy reasons, you probably should also look at other demographic variables as well to see if they predict the missingness (i.e., were males more likely to answer more questions than females, primary speaking language more likely to answer more, etc). Though these really don't effect the parameter estimation, directly in order to justify keeping them for the future you would want those to be non-significant as well (otherwise you'd bias the number of items administered for one sub-population over another...which is difficult to justify). Good luck.
>
> Phil

model_constrained <- mirt.model('

F2 = 6-12
COV = F1*F2

My intuition is to run a constrained model with the group argument in multipleGroup(), and then again look at the difficulty-parameters via a bivariate Wald-test, i.e.

group=c (rep ("D1", length (which (data$country=="US"))),

         rep ("D3", length (which (data$country=="CA"))))
mod_metric <- multipleGroup(data[,119:134], model_constrained, group = group,SE=T)

Any ideas if this is a good hunch? Am I correct that multipleGroup essentially fits different IRT models to different subsets of the data?

Tobi

messages.body_snippet: I found that the mixedmirt reported NAN standard error for many covariate parameters very often. However, the boot.mirt is not designed for mixedmirt. Any other work around to get standard error? Than

messages.subject: Re: mixedmirt (random intercept)
messages.body_plain:
Another small question. When I used cmod <- mixedmirt(data, covdata, cmodel, fixed = ~ 0, lr.fixed = list(F1=~eduGroup+ageGroup+genderGroup, F2=~eduGroup+ageGroup+genderGroup, F3=~eduGroup+ageGroup+genderGroup, F4=~eduGroup+ageGroup+genderGroup, F5=~eduGroup+ageGroup+genderGroup), itemtype='Rasch'), but the summary(cmod) seems missing the LATENT REGRESSION FIXED EFFECTS for F5 factor.

KK Sasa於 2014年12月7日星期日UTC+8下午12時18分07秒寫道：

> I found that the mixedmirt reported NAN standard error for many covariate parameters very often. However, the boot.mirt is not designed for mixedmirt. Any other work around to get standard error? Thanks.
>
> Phil Chalmers於 2014年12月5日星期五UTC+8下午2時11分05秒寫道：
> > I don't think it's possible. Missing values in the independent variables are pretty hard to deal with (same issue occurs in standard regression analyses). Probably the best approach would be to impute them using multiple imputation methods and average over multiple sets. Sorry.
> >
> > Phil
> >
> > On Fri, Dec 5, 2014 at 1:06 AM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Thank you, Phil. It seems mixedmirt does not allow missing values in continuous or categorical covariates. Will it support in the future? Say, missing at random?
> > >
> > > Phil Chalmers於 2014年12月4日星期四UTC+8下午12時10分19秒寫道：
> > > > Yes, the syntax looks good, and mixedmirt()'s lr.fixed input can tell how to use the variables (the standard R formula input deals with that using the usual R matrix.model() functions and such).
> > > >
> > > > Phil

> > > > > > > itemnum = 14
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Q <- array( 0 , dim = c( dim0*itemnum , dim0 ))
> > > > > > > ind = numeric()
> > > > > > > for (c in 1:dim0){

messages.subject: comparing two models (with/without data impuation)
messages.body_plain:
Hello Phil,

I want to fit a multidimensional GPCM to my data (2000 observations of 31 Likert-type items with 5 categories) in order to develop a multidimensional CAT.

First, I fitted the model to my data using this the following syntax:

mm = mirt(dat, model, "gpcm", method = "MHRM",  technical = list(MAXQUAD = 20000, NCYCLES = 1000))

Then, I estimated factor scores using MAP estimation (which is recommended to use when dealing with high numbers of latent traits) with the following syntax:

scores = fscores(mm, method = "MAP", full.scores = T)

In order to get complete response patterns for my incomplete observations (needed to perform CAT simulations), I fitted again the same model with imputed data:

mm2 = mirt(imputeMissing(mm,scores), model, "gpcm", method = "MHRM", technical = list(MAXQUAD = 20000, NCYCLES = 1000))

Finally, I printed the results of the two models:

> mm

Call:
mirt(data = dat, model = model, itemtype = "gpcm", method = "MHRM",
    technical = list(MAXQUAD = 20000, NCYCLES = 1000))

Full-information item factor analysis with 9 factor(s).
Converged within 0.001 tolerance after 940 MHRM iterations.
mirt version: 1.6.1
M-step optimizer: NR

Log-likelihood = -73479.22, SE = 0.104
AIC = 147334.4; AICc = 147373.8
BIC = 148386.7; SABIC = 147789.4

> mm2

Call:
mirt(data = imputeMissing(mm, scores), model = model, itemtype = "gpcm",
    method = "MHRM", technical = list(MAXQUAD = 20000, NCYCLES = 1000))

Full-information item factor analysis with 9 factor(s).
Converged within 0.001 tolerance after 915 MHRM iterations.
mirt version: 1.6.1
M-step optimizer: NR

Log-likelihood = -77555.71, SE = 0.096
AIC = 155487.4; AICc = 155526.8
BIC = 156539.6; SABIC = 155942.3

Given the information criteria (AIC and BIC), it seems that the first model (with incomplete data) is better than the second (with imputed data).

I would expect the opposite result, have you got an idea on this ?

Thank you.

Pierre

messages.body_plain:
Yes that seems like the right interpretation. Multiple-group (MG) methods are essentially a blend between two extremes: no group membership (ignoring it completely in the full datasets) and completely independent groups (equivalent to completely subsetting and analyzing independently with different mirt() runs). MG becomes beneficial when studying the relative equivalence of groups, and also allows linking of the groups by freeing things like latent variances and means (requires a certain amount of item-level constraints; but not many). Cheers.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: comparing two models (with/without data impuation)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Pierre,

This result seems perfectly reasonable to me. The datasets are not nested in the strict sense, so the data with no missing actually has more cases to work with, and, hence, a lower and more peaked log-likelihood. The same can be seen using just the default datasets:

```
dat <- expand.table(LSAT7)
(mod <- mirt(dat, 1))

dat[sample(1:length(dat), 100)] <- NA
(mod2 <- mirt(dat, 1))

(mod3 <- mirt(dat, 1, method = 'MHRM'))
````

Hope that helps.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Is it possbile to use mirt() instead of mixedmirt()? So that I can use bootstrap to get standard error. I tried

cmod <- mixedmirt(resp, covdata, cmodel, fixed = ~ 0, lr.fixed = list(F1=~ eduGroup, F2=~ eduGroup, F3=~ eduGroup, F4=~ eduGroup, F5=~ eduGroup), itemtype='Rasch')

It works. But,

cmod <- mirt(resp, cmodel, covdata=covdata, formula = list(F1=~ eduGroup, F2=~ eduGroup, F3=~ eduGroup, F4=~ eduGroup, F5=~ eduGroup) , itemtype='Rasch', SE=FALSE, method = "MHRM")
Error in MHRM.group(pars = pars, constrain = constrain, Ls = Ls, PrepList = PrepList,  :
  Constraint applied to fixed parameter(s) NA NA NA NA  but should only be applied to
                 estimated parameters. Please fix!
In addition: Warning message:
In estpars & !redun_constr :
  longer object length is not a multiple of shorter object length

failed. They are different?

Phil Chalmers於 2014年12月8日星期一UTC+8下午10時33分44秒寫道：

> I've noticed this happen as well, and am looking into better approaches. Decreasing the TOL criteria tends to help, or to obtain more stochastic information matrix draws pass a lower SEtol criteria to technical().
>
> Phil
>
> On Sat, Dec 6, 2014 at 11:18 PM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > I found that the mixedmirt reported NAN standard error for many covariate parameters very often. However, the boot.mirt is not designed for mixedmirt. Any other work around to get standard error? Thanks.
> >
> > Phil Chalmers於 2014年12月5日星期五UTC+8下午2時11分05秒寫道：
> > > I don't think it's possible. Missing values in the independent variables are pretty hard to deal with (same issue occurs in standard regression analyses). Probably the best approach would be to impute them using multiple imputation methods and average over multiple sets. Sorry.
> > >
> > > Phil
> > >
> > > On Fri, Dec 5, 2014 at 1:06 AM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Thank you, Phil. It seems mixedmirt does not allow missing values in continuous or categorical covariates. Will it support in the future? Say, missing at random?
> > > >
> > > > Phil Chalmers於 2014年12月4日星期四UTC+8下午12時10分19秒寫道：
> > > > > Yes, the syntax looks good, and mixedmirt()'s lr.fixed input can tell how to use the variables (the standard R formula input deals with that using the usual R matrix.model() functions and such).
> > > > >
> > > > > Phil
> > > > >
> > > > > On Wed, Dec 3, 2014 at 11:01 PM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > Thank you, Phil. Let say if adding covariate like gender (male and female) to second factor, I am not sure if mixedmirt(resp, covdata, cmodel, lr.fixed = list(F2=~ gender) ) is fine? Can lr.fixed tell the covariate is continuous or categorical?
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Phil Chalmers於 2014年12月3日星期三UTC+8下午12時46分55秒寫道：
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Tue, Dec 2, 2014 at 1:44 AM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > dim0 = 2
> > > > > > > > itemnum = 14
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Q <- array( 0 , dim = c( dim0*itemnum , dim0 ))
> > > > > > > > ind = numeric()
> > > > > > > > for (c in 1:dim0){
> > > > > > > >     ind = c( ind, rep(c,itemnum) )
> > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > Q[cbind(1:(dim0*itemnum), ind)] <- 1
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > COV = matrix(TRUE, dim0, dim0)
> > > > > > > > cmodel <- mirt.model(Q, COV=COV)

> > > > > > > > est = coef(cmod, printSE = TRUE, as.data.frame = TRUE)

> > > > > > > > But it estimated for F1 and F2:
> > > > > > > > $lr.betas

> > > > > > > > (Intercept) 0.000 0.000
> > > > > > > > pseudoIQ    0.041 0.516
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Patched now. Thanks.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Second, I tried to estimate all five-dimensional data with one covariate regressed on last dimension, pseudoIQ.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > dim0 = 5
> > > > > > > > itemnum = 14
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Q <- array( 0 , dim = c( dim0*itemnum , dim0 ))
> > > > > > > > ind = numeric()
> > > > > > > > for (c in 1:dim0){
> > > > > > > >     ind = c( ind, rep(c,itemnum) )
> > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > Q[cbind(1:(dim0*itemnum), ind)] <- 1
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > COV = matrix(TRUE, dim0, dim0)
> > > > > > > > cmodel <- mirt.model(Q, COV=COV)
> > > > > > > > pseudoIQ <- read.table("pseudoIQ.txt", col.names="pseudoIQ")
> > > > > > > > covdata <- data.frame(pseudoIQ)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > resp <- read.table("resp.txt")
> > > > > > > > cmod <- mirt(resp, cmodel, covdata=covdata, formula = list(F5=~ pseudoIQ) , itemtype='Rasch', SE=TRUE, method = "EM", SE.type="crossprod")
> > > > > > > > est = coef(cmod, printSE = TRUE, as.data.frame = TRUE)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > But there was a error:
> > > > > > > > Iteration: 22, Log-Lik: -48215.200, Max-Change: 0.04489Error in solve.default(sigma) :
> > > > > > > >   system is computationally singular: reciprocal condition number = 5.21813e-18
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > The latent variables in this model are quite highly correlated, and using EM estimation the quadrature become too problematic to deal with (the number of points is reduce to only 3 per dimension....so quite inaccurate). mixedmirt() seems to estimate this fine though, since the MHRM is generally better at dealing with high dimensional and multicollinear models. Cheers.

> > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Phil Chalmers於 2014年12月2日星期二UTC+8上午12時18分17秒寫道：
> > > > > > > > > Okay, this has been added. Simply pass a named list of formula to mirt(..., formula = list(...)) or mixedmirt(..., lr.fixed=list(...)), where the names correspond to the factor names defined in 'model'. Cheers.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > On Mon, Dec 1, 2014 at 1:26 AM, Phil Chalmers <rphilip....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > You need a fixed = ~ group + X, or whatever R formula added to that. Also, in mirt() the latent regression is only available for the EM algorithm (that's why the mirt and mixedmirt functions currently differ; the estimators deal with the problem rather differently). If you are running a later dev, there should be an example at the bottom of the ?mirt help file. Cheers.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > On Mon, Dec 1, 2014 at 1:22 AM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > Thanks, Phil. I have tried mirt() by including covariates:
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > covdata <- data.frame(pseudoIQ)
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > cmod <- mirt(resp, cmodel, covdata=covdata, itemtype='Rasch', SE=TRUE, method = "MHRM", technical=list(BURNIN=1000,SEMCYCLES=100,NCYCLES=10000), SE.type="")
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > coef(cmod)
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > But, I didn't see the estimate of coefficient.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Phil Chalmers於 2014年12月1日星期一UTC+8下午1時33分40秒寫道：
> > > > > > > > > > > > For the mirt() function, in theory yes, though I haven't implemented support for such an approach yet. Currently all regression coefficients are modelled for each trait at once. This probably meets your goal for now, at the cost of a slight decrease in power for including needless fixed effects.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > In mixedmirt(), the latest dev version can support this through the lr.fixed input, though it may be buggy as it is not well tested yet. And alternatively, if the model is Rasch then creating a suitable itemdesign effect for each factor and interacting it with the between-group effects would generate a suitable fixed/random coefficient to do the job.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > On Mon, Dec 1, 2014 at 12:17 AM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > Or alternatively can mirt() allows for covariates (latent regression)?
> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > Also yes, but does not support random effects (and probably never will). fscores() will also account for the latent structures in mirt(), allowing for plausible values and other related methods. Cheers.
> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > Assume my model is a three-dimensional model (one item measures only one dimension; between-item design) and I want to include covariates. Could I assign different covariates to the three dimensions respectively? For example, gender to dimension1, age to dimension 2, education to dimension 3. Thanks.

> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > Phil Chalmers於 2014年11月27日星期四UTC+8下午10時35分24秒寫道：
> > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > On Thu, Nov 27, 2014 at 3:08 AM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:

Ability decomposition support will be coming at a later time.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Or alternatively can mirt() allows for covariates (latent regression)?
> > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > Also yes, but does not support random effects (and probably never will). fscores() will also account for the latent structures in mirt(), allowing for plausible values and other related methods. Cheers.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Phil Chalmers於 2014年11月27日星期四UTC+8上午12時52分26秒寫道：
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Indeed, there was an inadvertent line of code causing issues in the draw variability (causing severe shrinkage towards the mean). This is now patched, and the simulation returns the following results now.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > summary(mod1)
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Call:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > mixedmirt(data = data, covdata = covdata, model = 1, fixed = ~0 +
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >     items, random = ~1 | group)
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > --------------
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > RANDOM EFFECT COVARIANCE(S):
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Correlations on upper diagonal
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > $Theta
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >     F1
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > F1 1.1
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > $group
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >           COV_group
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > COV_group     0.878
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > So the SD estimates are now sqrt(1.1) = 1.048, and sqrt(.878) = 0.937, which are much more reasonable. Thanks for the report!
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > On Tue, Nov 25, 2014 at 4:21 PM, Phil Chalmers <rphilip....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >

messages.subject: Re: mixedmirt (random intercept)
messages.body_plain:
No they are quite different, so this won't work (even if, you'd be mixing estimators). However, we can do one better. I've added support in boot.mirt to accept objects estimate with the MHRM, including mixedmirt() returns. If you weren't using parallel computing in boot.mirt before, I'd highly recommend doing that now if you pass an object that was estimated with method='MHRM'. Cheers.

Phil

On Tue, Dec 9, 2014 at 9:32 PM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Is it possbile to use mirt() instead of mixedmirt()? So that I can use bootstrap to get standard error. I tried
>
> cmod <- mixedmirt(resp, covdata, cmodel, fixed = ~ 0, lr.fixed = list(F1=~ eduGroup, F2=~ eduGroup, F3=~ eduGroup, F4=~ eduGroup, F5=~ eduGroup), itemtype='Rasch')
>
> It works. But,
>
> cmod <- mirt(resp, cmodel, covdata=covdata, formula = list(F1=~ eduGroup, F2=~ eduGroup, F3=~ eduGroup, F4=~ eduGroup, F5=~ eduGroup) , itemtype='Rasch', SE=FALSE, method = "MHRM")

> failed. They are different?

> > > > Phil

> > > > > > > > > > Okay, this has been added. Simply pass a named list of formula to mirt(..., formula = list(...)) or mixedmirt(..., lr.fixed=list(...)), where the names correspond to the factor names defined in 'model'. Cheers.

> > > > > > > > > > On Mon, Dec 1, 2014 at 1:26 AM, Phil Chalmers <rphilip....@gmail.com> wrote:

Also, in mirt() the latent regression is only available for the EM algorithm (that's why the mirt and mixedmirt functions currently differ; the estimators deal with the problem rather differently). If you are running a later dev, there should be an example at the bottom of the ?mirt help file. Cheers.

> > > > > > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > On Mon, Dec 1, 2014 at 1:22 AM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > > Thanks, Phil. I have tried mirt() by including covariates:
> > > > > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > cmod <- mirt(resp, cmodel, covdata=covdata, itemtype='Rasch', SE=TRUE, method = "MHRM", technical=list(BURNIN=1000,SEMCYCLES=100,NCYCLES=10000), SE.type="")

> > > > > > > > > > > > > In mixedmirt(), the latest dev version can support this through the lr.fixed input, though it may be buggy as it is not well tested yet. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Phil Chalmers於 2014年11月27日星期四UTC+8上午12時52分26秒寫道：

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > COV_group     0.878
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >

messages.subject: problem with mirtCAT function
messages.body_plain:
Hello Phil,

I fitted a multidimensional GPCM to my data using the mirt package, I estimated factor scores a first time. Then, in order to have complete response patterns (to perform CAT simualtions), I imputed the data and refitted the same model. Then I could run the mirtCAT function with all these outputs (here I generate a CAT using the first observation of my imputed data). Here is the corresponding script:

mm = mirt(dat, model, "gpcm", method = "MHRM",  technical = list(MAXQUAD = 20000, NCYCLES = 1000))

scores = fscores(mm, method = "MAP", full.scores = T)

dat_imput = imputeMissing(mm,scores)

mm2 = mirt(dat_imput, model, "gpcm", method = "MHRM", technical = list(MAXQUAD = 20000, NCYCLES = 1000))

mirtCAT(mirt_object = mm2, method = "MAP", criteria = "Drule", start_item = 1, local_pattern = dat_imput[1,])

My problem is that I got the following error message after running the mirtCAT function:

"Error in FI(extract.item(MCE$test$mirt_object, x), Theta = thetas) : Fisher-information matrix not currently supported for supplied classes"

Replacing the item selection criterion by "KL" solves the problem, but I would like to test different criteria and compare them to define the best way to administer my CAT. How can I use the information-based criteria ?

With the "KL" criterion, all the items are admnistered to reach the default 0.3 threshold for the SEM (which is not reached for all the dimensions), is there a reasonable standard in the literature for the SEM threshold ?

Hung & al (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23749433) proposes the value 3.3 as threshold but it seems weird given the SE take the values 1 at the first step of theta estimation....

Thank you for your help,

Best regards,

Pierre Michel.

Phil

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > --------------
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > RANDOM EFFECT COVARIANCE(S):
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Correlations on upper diagonal
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > $Theta
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >     F1
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > F1 1.1
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > $group
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >           COV_group
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > COV_group     0.878
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > So the SD estimates are now sqrt(1.1) = 1.048, and sqrt(.878) = 0.937, which are much more reasonable. Thanks for the report!
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > On Tue, Nov 25, 2014 at 4:21 PM, Phil Chalmers <rphilip....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > On Tue, Nov 25, 2014 at 3:21 AM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Hi Phil,
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > I experienced a hard time understanding what is working on behind mixedmirt. For simplicity, I simulated a random intercept data, where sample size 3000, group=200, using Rasch model, and the syntax is as follows:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > ~~~~~~
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > rm(list=ls())
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > set.seed(1234)
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > N <- 3000
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > a <- matrix(rep(1,10),10,1) # all ones
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > d <- matrix(seq(-2,2,length.out=10),10,1); d[1] = 0
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > cluster = 200
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > random_intercept = rnorm(cluster,0,1)
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Theta = numeric()
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > for (i in 1:cluster){
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >     Theta <- c(Theta, rnorm(N/cluster,0,1) + random_intercept[i])
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >     }
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > group = factor(rep(paste0('G',1:cluster), each = N/cluster))
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > covdata <- data.frame(group)
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > data <- simdata(a,d,N, itemtype = rep('dich',10), Theta=matrix(Theta))
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > mod1 <- mixedmirt(data, covdata, 1, fixed = ~ 0 + items, random = ~ 1|group)
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > coef(mod1, printSE = TRUE)
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > ~~~~~~
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > The item estimates were fine, but the variance of theta and variance of random intercept were not 1 and 1:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > $GroupPars
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >     MEAN_1 COV_11
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > par      0  1.727
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > SE      NA    NaN
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > $group
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >     COV_group_group
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > par           0.156
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > SE              NaN
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Not sure if I simulated incorrectly?
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > This looks like it should work, so I'm not sure why it isn't coming up with the correct estimates. I'll look into it and let you know what I find.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > How to estimate the mean of random intercept? (and put constrain on item estimate, overall mean is zero)
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > You can't, mainly because by convention random effects are generally thought to be centered at 0, and therefore I don't allow for them to be estimated. Cheers.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Thank you~
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >

messages.body_snippet:
Thanks for your hard work, Phil. The mirt manual does not provide details behind the scene of boot.mirt(), such as method used and references. Could you detail that?

Phil Chalmers於 2014年12月11日星期四UTC+

messages.subject: Re: mixedmirt (random intercept)
messages.body_plain:
See ?boot::boot.  boot.mirt() is just a specific handler which passes to that function (no need to reinvent the wheel). Cheers.

On Sat, Dec 13, 2014 at 12:10 AM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thanks for your hard work, Phil. The mirt manual does not provide details behind the scene of boot.mirt(), such as method used and references. Could you detail that?
>
> Phil Chalmers於 2014年12月11日星期四UTC+8上午2時13分27秒寫道：
> > No they are quite different, so this won't work (even if, you'd be mixing estimators). However, we can do one better. I've added support in boot.mirt to accept objects estimate with the MHRM, including mixedmirt() returns. If you weren't using parallel computing in boot.mirt before, I'd highly recommend doing that now if you pass an object that was estimated with method='MHRM'. Cheers.
> >
> > Phil
> >
> > On Tue, Dec 9, 2014 at 9:32 PM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Is it possbile to use mirt() instead of mixedmirt()? So that I can use bootstrap to get standard error. I tried
> > >
> > > cmod <- mixedmirt(resp, covdata, cmodel, fixed = ~ 0, lr.fixed = list(F1=~ eduGroup, F2=~ eduGroup, F3=~ eduGroup, F4=~ eduGroup, F5=~ eduGroup), itemtype='Rasch')
> > >
> > > It works. But,
> > >
> > > cmod <- mirt(resp, cmodel, covdata=covdata, formula = list(F1=~ eduGroup, F2=~ eduGroup, F3=~ eduGroup, F4=~ eduGroup, F5=~ eduGroup) , itemtype='Rasch', SE=FALSE, method = "MHRM")
> > > Error in MHRM.group(pars = pars, constrain = constrain, Ls = Ls, PrepList = PrepList,  :
> > >   Constraint applied to fixed parameter(s) NA NA NA NA  but should only be applied to
> > >                  estimated parameters. Please fix!
> > > In addition: Warning message:
> > > In estpars & !redun_constr :
> > >   longer object length is not a multiple of shorter object length
> > >
> > >
> > > failed. They are different?
> > >
> > >
> > > Phil Chalmers於 2014年12月8日星期一UTC+8下午10時33分44秒寫道：
> > > > I've noticed this happen as well, and am looking into better approaches. Decreasing the TOL criteria tends to help, or to obtain more stochastic information matrix draws pass a lower SEtol criteria to technical().
> > > >
> > > > Phil
> > > >
> > > > On Sat, Dec 6, 2014 at 11:18 PM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > I found that the mixedmirt reported NAN standard error for many covariate parameters very often. However, the boot.mirt is not designed for mixedmirt. Any other work around to get standard error? Thanks.
> > > > >
> > > > > Phil Chalmers於 2014年12月5日星期五UTC+8下午2時11分05秒寫道：
> > > > > > I don't think it's possible. Missing values in the independent variables are pretty hard to deal with (same issue occurs in standard regression analyses). Probably the best approach would be to impute them using multiple imputation methods and average over multiple sets. Sorry.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Phil
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Fri, Dec 5, 2014 at 1:06 AM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > Thank you, Phil. It seems mixedmirt does not allow missing values in continuous or categorical covariates. Will it support in the future? Say, missing at random?
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Phil Chalmers於 2014年12月4日星期四UTC+8下午12時10分19秒寫道：
> > > > > > > > Yes, the syntax looks good, and mixedmirt()'s lr.fixed input can tell how to use the variables (the standard R formula input deals with that using the usual R matrix.model() functions and such).
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > On Wed, Dec 3, 2014 at 11:01 PM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > Thank you, Phil. Let say if adding covariate like gender (male and female) to second factor, I am not sure if mixedmirt(resp, covdata, cmodel, lr.fixed = list(F2=~ gender) ) is fine? Can lr.fixed tell the covariate is continuous or categorical?
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Phil Chalmers於 2014年12月3日星期三UTC+8下午12時46分55秒寫道：
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > On Tue, Dec 2, 2014 at 1:44 AM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > I have five-dimensional data, every 14 items measure one dimension. First, I tried estimate the last two dimension with one covariate regressed on last dimension, pseudoIQ. Syntax is as follows:
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > dim0 = 2
> > > > > > > > > > > itemnum = 14
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Q <- array( 0 , dim = c( dim0*itemnum , dim0 ))
> > > > > > > > > > > ind = numeric()
> > > > > > > > > > > for (c in 1:dim0){
> > > > > > > > > > >     ind = c( ind, rep(c,itemnum) )
> > > > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > > > > Q[cbind(1:(dim0*itemnum), ind)] <- 1
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > COV = matrix(TRUE, dim0, dim0)
> > > > > > > > > > > cmodel <- mirt.model(Q, COV=COV)
> > > > > > > > > > > pseudoIQ <- read.table("pseudoIQ.txt", col.names="pseudoIQ")
> > > > > > > > > > > covdata <- data.frame(pseudoIQ)
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > resp <- read.table("resp.txt")
> > > > > > > > > > > cmod <- mirt(resp[,43:70], cmodel, covdata=covdata, formula = list(F2=~ pseudoIQ) , itemtype='Rasch', SE=TRUE, method = "EM", SE.type="crossprod")
> > > > > > > > > > > est = coef(cmod, printSE = TRUE, as.data.frame = TRUE)
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > But it estimated for F1 and F2:
> > > > > > > > > > > $lr.betas
> > > > > > > > > > >                F1    F2
> > > > > > > > > > > (Intercept) 0.000 0.000
> > > > > > > > > > > pseudoIQ    0.041 0.516
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Patched now. Thanks.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Second, I tried to estimate all five-dimensional data with one covariate regressed on last dimension, pseudoIQ.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > dim0 = 5
> > > > > > > > > > > itemnum = 14
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Q <- array( 0 , dim = c( dim0*itemnum , dim0 ))
> > > > > > > > > > > ind = numeric()
> > > > > > > > > > > for (c in 1:dim0){
> > > > > > > > > > >     ind = c( ind, rep(c,itemnum) )
> > > > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > > > > Q[cbind(1:(dim0*itemnum), ind)] <- 1
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > COV = matrix(TRUE, dim0, dim0)
> > > > > > > > > > > cmodel <- mirt.model(Q, COV=COV)
> > > > > > > > > > > pseudoIQ <- read.table("pseudoIQ.txt", col.names="pseudoIQ")
> > > > > > > > > > > covdata <- data.frame(pseudoIQ)
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > resp <- read.table("resp.txt")
> > > > > > > > > > > cmod <- mirt(resp, cmodel, covdata=covdata, formula = list(F5=~ pseudoIQ) , itemtype='Rasch', SE=TRUE, method = "EM", SE.type="crossprod")
> > > > > > > > > > > est = coef(cmod, printSE = TRUE, as.data.frame = TRUE)
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > But there was a error:
> > > > > > > > > > > Iteration: 22, Log-Lik: -48215.200, Max-Change: 0.04489Error in solve.default(sigma) :
> > > > > > > > > > >   system is computationally singular: reciprocal condition number = 5.21813e-18
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > The latent variables in this model are quite highly correlated, and using EM estimation the quadrature become too problematic to deal with (the number of points is reduce to only 3 per dimension....so quite inaccurate). mixedmirt() seems to estimate this fine though, since the MHRM is generally better at dealing with high dimensional and multicollinear models. Cheers.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Phil Chalmers於 2014年12月2日星期二UTC+8上午12時18分17秒寫道：
> > > > > > > > > > > > Okay, this has been added. Simply pass a named list of formula to mirt(..., formula = list(...)) or mixedmirt(..., lr.fixed=list(...)), where the names correspond to the factor names defined in 'model'. Cheers.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > On Mon, Dec 1, 2014 at 1:26 AM, Phil Chalmers <rphilip....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > You need a fixed = ~ group + X, or whatever R formula added to that. Also, in mirt() the latent regression is only available for the EM algorithm (that's why the mirt and mixedmirt functions currently differ; the estimators deal with the problem rather differently). If you are running a later dev, there should be an example at the bottom of the ?mirt help file. Cheers.
> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > On Mon, Dec 1, 2014 at 1:22 AM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > Thanks, Phil. I have tried mirt() by including covariates:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > covdata <- data.frame(pseudoIQ)
> > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > cmod <- mirt(resp, cmodel, covdata=covdata, itemtype='Rasch', SE=TRUE, method = "MHRM", technical=list(BURNIN=1000,SEMCYCLES=100,NCYCLES=10000), SE.type="")
> > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > coef(cmod)
> > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > But, I didn't see the estimate of coefficient.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > Phil Chalmers於 2014年12月1日星期一UTC+8下午1時33分40秒寫道：
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > For the mirt() function, in theory yes, though I haven't implemented support for such an approach yet. Currently all regression coefficients are modelled for each trait at once. This probably meets your goal for now, at the cost of a slight decrease in power for including needless fixed effects.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > In mixedmirt(), the latest dev version can support this through the lr.fixed input, though it may be buggy as it is not well tested yet. And alternatively, if the model is Rasch then creating a suitable itemdesign effect for each factor and interacting it with the between-group effects would generate a suitable fixed/random coefficient to do the job.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > On Mon, Dec 1, 2014 at 12:17 AM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Or alternatively can mirt() allows for covariates (latent regression)?
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Also yes, but does not support random effects (and probably never will). fscores() will also account for the latent structures in mirt(), allowing for plausible values and other related methods. Cheers.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Assume my model is a three-dimensional model (one item measures only one dimension; between-item design) and I want to include covariates. Could I assign different covariates to the three dimensions respectively? For example, gender to dimension1, age to dimension 2, education to dimension 3. Thanks.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Phil Chalmers於 2014年11月27日星期四UTC+8下午10時35分24秒寫道：
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > On Thu, Nov 27, 2014 at 3:08 AM, KK Sasa <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Thank you, Phil. Now it works well. By the way, can mixedmirt() handle multidimensional IRT? Say, only one major trait is treated in multilevel structure and others are ignored.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Yes, but specific decomposition of the traits is not yet supported. One can get around this by including general intercept differences, but these will largely be agnostic to the multidimensional traits used (which has pros and cons). Ability decomposition support will be coming at a later time.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Or alternatively can mirt() allows for covariates (latent regression)?
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Also yes, but does not support random effects (and probably never will). fscores() will also account for the latent structures in mirt(), allowing for plausible values and other related methods. Cheers.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Indeed, there was an inadvertent line of code causing issues in the draw variability (causing severe shrinkage towards the mean). This is now patched, and the simulation returns the following results now.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > summary(mod1)
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >     items, random = ~1 | group)
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > --------------
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > RANDOM EFFECT COVARIANCE(S):

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > $Theta

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >

The elements can still be obtained from coef() (meaning they were estimated), but summary() will miss their values). The printout fix for this has been pushed to the dev version.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Monotonically decreasing function
messages.body_plain:
Hi Danilo,

It depends on the nature of the items, which we don't know. You'd have to look at why these have negative or not slopes (are they reverse scored, measure a distinct factor, have dramatically different content compared to other items, etc). In any case, definitely do not use a Rasch model since that is very very bad. The Rasch model fixes all the slopes to be equal by definition, so it will fit these data incredible poorly (stats like M2() and itemfit() will make this apparent, but you'll also see a massive drop in things like BIC/AIC and the log-likelihoods).

Regarding the 3PL model, unless you have a huge amount of data (2000+ individuals) you'll need to include normal priors on the lower bound parameters to keep them stable. It's a common problem with that model, and freely estimating the g parameters is generally not recommended. Cheers.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Methods for checking the unidimensionality
messages.body_plain:
You don't have to use confirmatory models to check dimensionality, you can just use exploratory ones (pass a # to the model input). Comparing things like AIC and BIC are useful here, and will correspond quite well to a scree plot with a polychoric correlation matrix. See help(psych::fa.parallel.poly) for a limited information variant of this approach.

Phil

Hi,

I'm studying bi-factor model and today I have a (unclear) question.

I think bifactor model belongs to so called hierarchical factor analysis model(sometimes higher order analysis model).

If so, don't parameter estimation in bifactor model have identifiability problems?

for example, we have to restrict item discrimination parameter in some item (at least 1 item) to 0 ?

But I also think that Gibbons&Hedeker (1992)' method;
 Gibbons&Hedeker (1992) say that the bifactor restriction reduces the s-dimensional integral in (4) to a two dimensional integral...

So, using  Gibbons&Hedeker (1992)' method, we don't have restrict a parameter in some item to 0?

This question seems to be difficult to understand because of my lack of studies.

If you have some opinion, please give me that.

Thank you,

Yutaro

There are generally 2 ways to identify random variables: fix a slope to some constant (usually 1), or fix the variance to a constant (also to 1). Either will suffice for identification, and the latter is what Gibbons and Hedeker use to accomplish the dimensional reduction technique. Cheers.

messages.subject: Re: Identifiability Problems in bi-factor model
messages.body_plain:
Yes. Computationally, standardized orthogonal integrals can be 'short formed' if you will to reduce computational complexity in high dimensional spaces. That's why in their solution no matter how many specific factors that are estimated, only 2 dimensional integration is required. But they aren't really taken to be N(0, 1) per say, that's just an identification constraint required (and is exactly the same as in structural equation modeling).

Phil
